default: It is a morning, some years later.

You are in the market square at Crestfall, and the fountain is running properly now. Somebody mended it in the second year. It took three weeks, the whole town had an opinion about it, and Aldous paid for half of it and will not admit that he did.

There are nine stalls in the market. The ninth is new. It belongs to a woman from one of the villages to the east, who walked out of the forest again eighteen months after she walked into it, bewildered and thin, and in the end, little by little, herself again. She sells dried herbs. Some of them come from Maret's garden, and some are kinds nobody knew until she began to grow them.

default.text: You and [missing person] live in the house on the north lane, Goran's old house, which came free two years after you decided to stay. You have lived there ever since.
default.else: You and [missing person] live in the house on the north lane with the blue door, which came free two years after you decided to stay. You have lived there ever since.

default: This morning there is the market, and the fountain, and the light that comes over Crestfall at this time of year. It isn't warm, exactly. It is plainer than that. You are standing in it, and so is [missing person], and the day hasn't yet told you what it wants of you.

default.text: Some evenings [missing person] still walks the east field fence with one foot on the rail, and still waits for you to fall off first.
Some nights [missing person] reads by the lamp with their knees drawn up, and you pretend to be asleep.
[missing person] has the back room, over the yard, and the two of you argue about the shutters.
[missing person] still corrects your work, and you still let them.
[missing person] waits up when you are late, and you are late less often.
You said it in the end, one ordinary evening by the mill wall, and [missing person] said they knew.
Once a month you and [missing person] walk east to the chamber and sit with the seal for an afternoon. It hasn't finished, and it hasn't failed.
Once a month a keeper in plain grey walks the east road to the chamber and back. Edric has stopped saying "cleansed".
Order came back first. The camp is smaller now, and it files reports.
Crestfall went still once, before the seal held. Most of it came back. Aldous sits by the fire most evenings now, and somebody else keeps the bar.

text.commander:
You have a proper post now. It isn't the one the Compact offered; it is something more to the purpose. There is a small body charged with the recovery of the whole region, and you chair it. Maret sits on it and Pol advises it. Branch doesn't sit on it, because Branch doesn't sit on things, but he is always there when he is wanted.

You have done harder work with less to do it with, and work that mattered less with more. This is the right work, on the right scale, with the right people, and you have the satisfaction of somebody doing what they were made for.
text.arcane:
The account has become a book, and it has been in print for two years. You have letters about it from scholars in four countries, and from ordinary people who read it because they heard there was a book about what happened in Ashenveld.

[missing person], whose fourteen months made most of what is in it possible, has their name on the cover. They don't mind. They stopped needing some things in the ruins, and have not started needing them again.
text.ranger:
The forest east of Crestfall is not the forest it was three years ago. You wouldn't say it was restored; that would mean it had gone back to how it was, and forests don't go back, they go on. But it works. The wolves came back in the third year, and it is a forest that works as a forest should.

You still read it every morning. The record you have kept is the fullest account anywhere of a country mending from a kind of harm nobody had seen before.

Some mornings [missing person] comes with you. They read the land with you as you read people, looking for what is true under what it shows. They are not at all bad at it.
text.cipher:
Things in Ashenveld are steady now, as they are when people have put enough into something that they don't want to lose it.

Maret is the most trusted person in the region, and Branch the most capable. Lira, of all people, is becoming a teacher. She found that the ways she learned of managing her own mind are just as good for helping other people manage theirs.

You watch it all with the satisfaction of somebody who built a thing and can see it working.

[missing person], standing beside you in the morning light in the market, says, "You are taking notes again."

"Yes," you say.

"Good," they say.

choices.text: Stay in the morning. Let the day arrive.

default.text:
You stay.

The day comes on as days do, without any notion that it might matter.

There is the market, and the fountain, and the nine stalls, and the light, and [missing person], and the years it took to make this morning.

Nothing ends. It simply goes on, as real things go on, without any fuss and without stopping. You chose that.

The end.

text.default:
It is a morning some time later. It is not years. It is months, long enough for things to have settled into a way of going on.

You are somewhere that doesn't know your name and has no need to. It is pleasant to be somewhere that nothing you did ever touched.

[missing person] is beside you, having breakfast, in a market town they chose because they heard the birds here were interesting. The birds are interesting. They were right.

Letters come from Ashenveld every fortnight, from Maret and Branch and Pol. The mending goes on, and the work goes on without you. That is what you built: something that could go on without you.

default: Across the table [missing person] is eating bread and butter, slowly, as though it were a feast.
You watch them eat their breakfast in a town they chose. It is not what you thought your life would look like. You are not sure what you thought it would look like. But here you are.

default.text: [missing person] has found a fence to walk along here too.
You say goodbye properly now, to every town you leave, and [missing person] watches you do it.
Every month the two of you write a line each to your mother, and post it nowhere.
[missing person] is teaching somebody else now, and lets you watch.
[missing person] still asks whether you have been eating.
You said it on the road, in the second week, and [missing person] said they knew.
Pol walks east to the chamber every new moon and writes to tell you what she finds. Her letters are short. Holding, they say. Not finished.
Once a month a keeper in plain grey walks the east road to the chamber and back. Edric has stopped saying "cleansed".
The last you see of that market town is the road out of it, going east. You walk it together, and neither of you hurries.
There is one thing you still haven't said to them. There is time.
Crestfall went still once, before the seal held. Most of it came back. Aldous sits by the fire most evenings now, and somebody else keeps the bar.

text.commander:
You are not in command of anything at present, which is a new state of affairs.

You are finding that the knack of command doesn't go when there is nothing to command. It turns into something else: you notice things, and you are exact, and you can read a situation quickly. Those are as useful in ordinary life. They are only useful differently.
text.arcane:
You are writing again. It isn't the account of Ashenveld, which is finished. It is something new, the beginning of a longer work about what the ruins were and what the power was, and what the ritual might tell people about things that have been seen in other places and never understood.

Ashenveld is not the only such place. You always knew it in principle. Now you are beginning to know it in fact.

[missing person] reads your drafts and asks questions that make them better. They spent fourteen months in the richest place for your kind of study that there has ever been. If they wanted to be, they could be a scholar of real note.

You ask whether they want to be. They think about it, and say: sometimes.
text.ranger:
The forest round here is not like Ashenveld's. It is ordinary and unharmed, and it has the richness of country that never went through what Ashenveld went through.

You read it every morning all the same. You can't stop reading the land, and you have given up minding.

[missing person] has started coming with you. They are learning to read the land as you do, looking for what is true under what it shows. They are not bad at it. They spent fourteen months reading some of the hardest country there is, and the knack has carried over.
text.cipher:
Now that you are out of Ashenveld, with no scheming to manage, you have found something out. You are good company when you aren't managing anything.

It surprises you more than it surprises [missing person], who seems to have known it all along.

"You are different out here," they say.

"Yes," you say.

"It suits you," they say. You take that in, and keep it.

default.text:
The day goes on, ordinary and particular.

Ashenveld is behind you, but what you learned there isn't. You carry it as you carry anything that has changed you. It isn't a burden, and it isn't a trophy. It is simply that you notice things you never used to notice.

The birds here are interesting.

[missing person] finishes their breakfast, and looks up, and sees you watching them.

"What?" they say.

"Nothing," you say. "Just looking."

They let it pass. They have let a good deal pass, where you are concerned. You mean to deserve it.

The end.

text.default:
It is a morning, several years later.

You are in the market square at Crestfall. The fountain is running, and has been for two years. There are nine stalls, and there are children who know the curse only as a story their parents tell.

The children call you the Warden. Nobody gave you the name. It simply grew up, as names do in small places, because you were always there, always doing whatever wanted doing, and always seemed to know the answer to whatever the town was asking.

You aren't sure you like it. You have stopped trying to change it.

This morning there is the market, and the fountain, and the children who never heard the wrong silence because they were too young, or not born. There is the Rootless camp, which is a proper body now, with a building and a sign and Lira on the staff. Branch is somewhere about its edges, doing whatever Branch does there.

Maret crosses the square, sees you, and lifts a hand. You have worked together so long that neither of you needs to say good morning.

default.text: Twice a year a letter comes from [missing person], and you answer every one.
[missing person] writes in the spring. You keep the letters in the drawer by the bed.
[missing person] writes from the coast that they keep a room for you, and you keep not using it.
[missing person] sends you questions by letter, and you send back answers they already know.
In every letter [missing person] writes that they are proud of you, and you have stopped arguing.
You never said it. [missing person] writes all the same, and doesn't ask.
On the first of every month you walk east to the chamber alone and listen to the note. It is quieter every year. It has never stopped.
Once a month a keeper in plain grey walks the east road to the chamber and back. Edric has stopped saying "cleansed".
At every new moon you read Maret the first line. She listens as if it were news.
The days are shorter for you now. Lira carries the ledger.
Crestfall went still once, before the seal held. Most of it came back. Aldous sits by the fire most evenings now, and somebody else keeps the bar.

text.commander:
You took the Compact's offer in the end, though you altered it first, and made it into something you could accept without giving up the freedom the work needs.

The body that sees to the region's recovery exists because you built it. It works because Maret runs the people and you run the institution, and the two of you, against all likelihood, trust each other.

You have not made your peace with being here alone. You have made your peace with the work being worth doing anyway.
text.arcane:
The account became a book, and the book is taught at three universities. Students who have read it write to you wanting to know more.

Some years ago a letter came from a town three weeks west of Ashenveld. It was not from the person you hoped. It was from a scholar [missing person] had sent the book to, who wanted to talk to you about something like it in their own part of the world.

You wrote back, and you have been writing to each other ever since. The work goes further than Ashenveld. Whether that is a comfort or a distraction you haven't decided, and you have stopped minding which.
text.ranger:
The hawk's descendants have territories of their own now. You know three of them by their markings, and by where they hunt.

The forest east of Crestfall works. It doesn't work as it did before the curse; it works differently. There are creatures here now that were never here before. The curse changed the land, and the land went on changing after the curse stopped. What it has become is not the old forest back again. It is the next forest.

You read it every morning, and have done for years. Nobody knows this country as well as you do. When you are gone, the record you have kept will be all that is left of what you knew.

That troubles you sometimes. You have been teaching Branch's youngest to read the forest. He isn't bad at it.
text.cipher:
Things in Ashenveld settled long ago, past the point where they need you to manage them.

What they need now is for you to be here. You were there when it mattered, and you stayed when somebody had to, and that gives you a weight in the place.

You aren't naive about it. You know how it works. You have held this place together so long that you have become part of it, rather than somebody acting on it.

There are worse things to become. You have decided to be this, without pretending you chose it quite freely. Some choices make themselves, a little at a time. You notice that, and then you go to the market and do another day's work.

choices.text: Let the morning be what it is.

default.text:
Maret crosses the square and lifts a hand, and you lift yours.

She walks on, and you stay where you are.

There is the fountain, and the children, and the hawk somewhere above the ordinary forest to the east.

You are the Warden of Ashenveld. It is not what you came here to be. It is what happened because you kept on staying.

Somewhere to the west of here, the person you came back to Ashenveld for is having a morning that you are no part of. You know it, and it is part of this morning, along with everything else.

The day begins.

The end.

default: Years have gone by. Crestfall has a name in the region now, not a famous one, but known. It is the town where the curse was stopped, the town with the camp that knows what to do when somebody comes out of the forest changed.

The Rootless camp isn't called the Rootless camp any more. It has a proper name, the Ashenveld Recovery Centre, which took three meetings to agree on and which nobody uses except on official papers. Everyone still calls it the camp. Maret is still Maret.
You and [missing person] are part of it, part of all of it: the work, and the place, and a life made in a hard country with the people who stayed.
It was not the easy way, and it was not the way the institutions wanted. It was the way that put the people who knew most about the curse in charge of what came after it.

default.text: You and [missing person] walk the camp's fence most evenings, as you once walked the east field.
[missing person] keeps the camp's ledgers by lamplight, with their knees drawn up, and you still pretend to be asleep.
You and [missing person] share a hut at the edge of the camp, and the same old arguments.
[missing person] teaches the camp's young ones what they once taught you, and some evenings asks you to take the class.
[missing person] sits by the camp fire most nights until you come in from the edge, and you always do.
You said it the first winter at the camp, and [missing person] said they had known for twenty years.
The camp keeps a rota for the walk east. Branch goes most months. He comes back and says "Holding," and nothing else.
Once a month a keeper in plain grey walks the east road to the chamber and back. Edric has stopped saying "cleansed".
Crestfall went still once, before the seal held. Most of it came back. Aldous sits by the fire most evenings now, and somebody else keeps the bar.

text.commander:
The body that runs the region's recovery answers to a civilian board, not to the Compact. That was the longest negotiation of all, and it cost you more goodwill than any other, and it was the one that mattered most.

Vorne went on to another region three years ago. Now and then he sends a letter. His letters are formal, and not frequent, and warm in the way soldiers' letters are warm. They say what was done, and don't dwell on it.

You answer in the same way. You were opponents and allies and never quite either, and the letters show it.
text.arcane:
What the ruins are, and what the seal did, is known to everyone now, and complete, and nobody owns it. That was the most important thing you did, and the thing most likely to be forgotten. It was not the knowledge itself. It was making sure nobody could ever keep it to themselves.

You teach now, as well as write. Students come to Ashenveld, and the place itself is the lesson. You know more about it than anyone else who is willing to stand in it with students and let them ask questions.

It is the best work you have ever done as a scholar.
text.ranger:
The camp has a garden that grows what the villages round about need. Lira laid it out. She knows which plants draw off what the curse left behind, and which help the afflicted who are still mending, and which are simply good for people to grow and look after.

You helped with the first survey of the ground. The garden is Lira's.

That is how the work goes when it is done properly. You do your part, and stand back, and the people who know their parts do theirs, and what comes of it is better than anything one person could have planned.
text.cipher:
Siding with the Rootless was right. It wasn't that the others were wrong. It was that the camp understood best what Ashenveld needed, and had most reason to get it right.

To side with the people with most reason to get it right is not being idealistic. It is simply good judgement, and your judgement was good.

Over the years you have also come to care about the camp doing well, in ways that have nothing to do with judgement. You leave that untidy.

default.text:
There is the camp, and the town, and the work.

You are the warden. Nobody gave you the title. You stayed long enough to become the person the place grew round.

Ashenveld goes on, and the curse goes back. The people who went east and came back keep on coming back, slowly, as people do who have been a long way inside themselves.

The ones who haven't come back you keep in a separate place. There is Joren, who is at the camp and mending and still doesn't always speak. There are the others, who went further. There is Wren, who has not come back and may never.

You keep all of it: what worked and what didn't, what was done and what was left. And there is the morning light over Crestfall, which is the same light it always was, and which at last, after all this time, you can look at without wondering what the curse is doing to it.

The end.

text.default:
The account was published in the second year.

It was not the scholars' account; that went to the universities. This was something else. It was a full record of what happened in Ashenveld: what each of the powers did and why, what the Covenant's purification would have cost, what Seriva did twenty years ago and what came of it, what the Compact was really doing here, and what the Rootless camp managed with no money and no recognition.

Every name was in it, and every decision, and every thing that had been hidden.

Ashenveld read it, and so did the region. The Compact made a formal reply, and so did the Covenant. Seriva made none.

The formal replies mattered less than the rest. The people who had lived through the curse had, at last, a full account of what had been done to them, and of who had decided what while it was happening.

Nobody came out of it with all the credit, and nobody came out of it clean. What came out of it was the truth, in everybody's hands, which was what you meant.

default: Ashenveld didn't fall apart. It broke up into smaller places, each of them gathered round whoever was most trusted there. Maret's camp became the middle of a loose web of villages that managed without anybody in charge, and, after the first hard years, found they didn't need anybody.
It was lonely work. More people know the truth because of it.

default.text: [missing person] read every page before it went to the printer, and argued with you about two of them.
[missing person] wrote the last chapter. You never asked them to change a word of it.
[missing person]'s name is in the account beside yours, in the order your mother would have put them.
[missing person] corrected your drafts in the margins, as they used to correct everything.
[missing person] keeps a copy on the shelf by the door, where visitors can see it.
The account has a dedication. It is one line long, and [missing person] has never mentioned it.
The last page of the account says who goes to look at the seal: Pol, and Lira after her, once a month. It says the seal is only partly made. It says so plainly.
Once a month a keeper in plain grey walks the east road to the chamber and back. Edric has stopped saying "cleansed".
Crestfall went still once, before the seal held. Most of it came back. Aldous sits by the fire most evenings now, and somebody else keeps the bar.

text.commander:
You published the account knowing it would cost you every connection you had with every institution, and it did.

Vorne stopped writing. The Compact formally struck you off as an adviser. Edric, to his credit, wrote to say the account was accurate, and that being accurate was the only reason the Covenant could begin to mend what it had become.

You belong to no institution now. You belong to the truth, which is a smaller body, but the company is good.
text.arcane:
What the scholars made of the account was the most interesting part of it.

They accepted the scholars' version. The other account, the full record of what institutions had failed to do and what had been hidden, began an argument that will go on for decades. Nobody argues about whether it is accurate. They argue about whether it ought to have been published.

You believe it ought. You also think they are right to argue about it, and you find you don't mind that they do.
text.ranger:
You published the account and watched Ashenveld take it in.

It didn't happen all at once. The truth goes round small places slowly. Each person reads it alongside what they already knew, and has to think again about things they lived through.

The replies that mattered most were the quiet ones. There were people who had known something was wrong and now knew the whole of it. There were people who had trusted an institution that the account showed had not deserved it, and who now had to decide what to do about that.

Most of them did what people in hard places always do. They carried on. The account didn't put anything right. It told the truth about what needed putting right, which is a different sort of help.
text.cipher:
The account was the biggest thing you ever did with what you knew.

When you published it you knew you were throwing away any standing you had in Ashenveld, for good. You published it all the same.

You have wondered why more often than you have wondered about nearly anything. The answer you keep coming back to is a simple one: the truth mattered more than your standing. It is not a complicated answer. It is only a hard one to live with.

You live with it.

choices.text: The account is out, and the truth is in the world.

default.text:
The morning after the account came out, you walked down to the market square.

Crestfall was reading it; you could see that. People had copies, and were talking quietly together. Aldous was behind the bar with his own copy, shut, with his hand resting on the cover.

You sat at your usual table, and Aldous brought you something without being asked.

[missing person] sat down across from you. They had read it, of course. They were in it, a good deal. They had read it, and they were sitting across from you looking at you, and they understood exactly what you had done.

"Was it right?" you asked.

"Yes," they said. "It was right. It will not make you many friends."

Ashenveld would go on, smaller and less certain and more honest. The people who lived there would know what had been done to them, and the people who had decided things while it was happening would be known.

You finished your drink, and Aldous didn't charge you for it.

The end.
